meta.description: Dorothy Parker, in a 1943 review of Lucius Beebe. She wrote “a book”, not “an item” — and Walter Winchell only repeated her.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Gift Book Is an Item Which You Wouldn't Take on Any Other Terms'?
meta.ogDescription: Dorothy Parker, Saturday Review of Literature, 11 December 1943, page 11. The word she used was “book”; “item” came later.

answer.label: Not quite — Dorothy Parker wrote “a book”, not “an item”
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer; founding member of the Algonquin Round Table
answer.sourceLine: Dorothy Parker wrote it, and we know exactly where. Reviewing Lucius Beebe’s Snoot If You Must under the title “The Trough of Plenty” in the Saturday Review of Literature of 11 December 1943, page 11, she wrote: “It must be what I believe is known as a gift book. That is to say, a book which you wouldn’t take on any other terms.” The version in circulation swaps her “book” for “an item” — a word Quote Investigator ↗ finds in none of the sources it cites.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the right author and a documented source, but not the words people quote.

source.excerpt: It must be what I believe is known as a gift book. That is to say, a book which you wouldn’t take on any other terms.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ gives the earliest citation as Dorothy Parker’s review “The Trough of Plenty” of Lucius Beebe’s Snoot If You Must, in the Saturday Review of Literature of 11 December 1943, page 11, and reproduces her sentence in full.

Walter Winchell is in the story, but as a megaphone rather than an author. QI: “Parker’s review was noticed by influential commentator Walter Winchell who repeated the quip in his widely-read column in January 1944.” The column of 3 January 1944 names her outright — “D. Parker in the Sat. Review cracks down on Luke Beebe’s tome… ‘That is to say,’ Dotty sabers, ‘a book you wouldn’t take on any other terms.’”

The line then passes into the quotation books with Parker’s name attached and her wording intact: Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me (1944), page 111, then The Algonquin Wits (1968) and Not Much Fun: The Lost Poems of Dorothy Parker (1996). Every one of them says “a book”.

On the wording we asked Quote Investigator directly: the word “item” appears in its headline for the piece, and in none of the sources the piece cites. So the familiar form is a later smoothing of a review sentence, not a quotation of one.

We read Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page ↗ in full — it maintains separate Quotes, Attributed and Misattributed sections. The gift-book line appears in none of them, in either wording. Dates checked independently: Parker, 22 August 1893 – 7 June 1967 ↗, Winchell, 7 April 1897 – 20 February 1972 ↗, and Beebe, 9 December 1902 – 4 February 1966 ↗
source.cutTag: Dorothy Parker on Lucius Beebe, 11 December 1943
source.excerptNote: This is a review sentence, not an aphorism: Parker is not defining gift books in general, she is disposing of one particular book by one particular man. Quote Investigator ↗ reproduces the passage from page 11 of the Saturday Review of Literature; we could not consult the 1943 issue ourselves.

author.bio: Dorothy Parker (née Rothschild, 1893–1967) was an American poet, critic and writer of fiction, based in New York and known for her caustic wisecracks and her eye for twentieth-century urban foibles. She was a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table and published in magazines including The New Yorker; in the early 1930s she went to Hollywood to write screenplays, earning two Academy Award nominations. The gift-book line comes from the reviewing that made her name.

misattribution.heading: Often mis-worded, and sometimes mis-credited
misattribution.intro: Two things have happened to this line on its way to you: it lost a word, and it picked up a second name.

items.why: Parker was reviewing a book and wrote “a book”. The generalised form — “a gift book is an item which you wouldn’t take on any other terms” — turns a specific insult into a general maxim. Quote Investigator ↗ confirms the word “item” is in none of the sources it cites; every citation from 1943 to 1996 reads “book”.

Winchell was a nationally famous syndicated gossip columnist, and his column of 3 January 1944 carried the joke far beyond the Saturday Review’s readership — which is how a repeater’s name comes to travel with a line. But he was quoting, and said so: he named Parker, named her review, and put her words in quotation marks. QI credits him with repeating the quip, never with coining it ↗

Beebe — writer, gourmand, railroad historian and columnist — wrote the book Parker was reviewing, Snoot If You Must. He is the person the line was aimed at, which occasionally gets him listed alongside it. QI’s verdict ↗: “Dorothy Parker did bare her fangs and Lucius Beebe did feel her venom.”

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: Dorothy Parker, “The Trough of Plenty,” Saturday Review of Literature, 11 December 1943, page 11 — the earliest documented source, per Quote Investigator ↗, which reproduces her sentence in full.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Parker had made her name writing for magazines including The New Yorker, and as a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table — a reputation for sharp wit she herself deplored. By 1943 she was famous enough that a single sentence could follow a book around for years afterwards, which is roughly what happened to Snoot If You Must.

Quote Investigator ends on the odd double effect of that kind of wit, borrowing a line from Somerset Maugham: “Helen could make a scholar immortal with a kiss; she (Dorothy Parker) can make a fool immortal with a jibe.”
context.pull: Beebe is remembered for the book. The book is remembered for the sentence about it.

schema.verdictNote: Dorothy Parker is the author, and the source is documented — her review of Lucius Beebe in the Saturday Review of Literature, 11 December 1943. This popular wording is not what she wrote: she wrote “a book which you wouldn’t take on any other terms”, not “an item”.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI gives the earliest citation as Dorothy Parker's review 'The Trough of Plenty' of Lucius Beebe's Snoot If You Must, Saturday Review of Literature, 11 December 1943, page 11, and reproduces: 'It must be what I believe is known as a gift book. That is to say, a book which you wouldn't take on any other terms.'

QI: 'Parker's review was noticed by influential commentator Walter Winchell who repeated the quip in his widely-read column in January 1944.' The column of 3 January 1944 credits Parker by name. QI never credits Winchell with coining it.
QI's later citations are Bennett Cerf, Try and Stop Me (1944), page 111; The Algonquin Wits (1968); and Not Much Fun: The Lost Poems of Dorothy Parker (1996) - all giving 'a book', crediting Parker.
The word 'item' appears in QI's headline for the article but in none of the sources the article cites.

QI's conclusion: 'Dorothy Parker did bare her fangs and Lucius Beebe did feel her venom... As author Somerset Maugham noted: Helen could make a scholar immortal with a kiss; she (Dorothy Parker) can make a fool immortal with a jibe.'
Wikiquote's Dorothy Parker page carries Quotes, Attributed and Misattributed sections and contains no instance of the gift-book line in any of them.

Dorothy Parker (nee Rothschild, 22 August 1893 - 7 June 1967) was an American poet, literary critic and writer of fiction, a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, published in The New Yorker, and earned two Academy Award nominations as a Hollywood screenwriter.
Walter Winchell (7 April 1897 - 20 February 1972) was an American syndicated newspaper gossip columnist and radio news commentator who rose to national celebrity in the 1930s.
Lucius Morris Beebe (9 December 1902 - 4 February 1966) was an American writer, gourmand, photographer, railroad historian, journalist and syndicated columnist.
